headline: SW Ledge Slack at 6:40: Bass Are Pinning Bunker Against the Rock
subhead: Two days off the new moon, the tide's running hard through SW Ledge and stripers are using it — bonito and albies are still a no-show, but the setup says soon.
body_markdown:
6:40 AM. That's slack before the ebb at SW Ledge this week, and if you're not anchored up or drifting the top of the rock by 6:20, you've already missed the best fifteen minutes of the morning. I had the boat parked in 28 feet on the northwest corner Tuesday, right where the ledge drops from 18 down into the channel, and watched the sounder light up with peanut bunker getting pushed and pinched against the rock as the current built. Two minutes later the marks scattered and the rod bent. That's the whole game out there right now — read the bait, read the tide, be in position before the water starts moving.

We flagged this last week — said building tidal flow into the August 12 new moon would sharpen the bite at current-driven structure, and that's exactly what's playing out at SW Ledge and down around Sandy Point. The spring tides off this moon are shoving more water through the rip than we've seen all summer, and it's dragging bunker schools right into the teeth of it. Stripers from 26 inches up to a genuine 35-pounder — landed Wednesday on a chunk of fresh bunker fished on a fish-finder rig in 40 feet on the down-current side — are using that current like a conveyor belt. If you're throwing artificials, a white or bone SP Minnow worked with a stall-and-twitch on the up-tide swing has been drawing the better fish, and bucktails in the 2-ounce range, white with a white curly tail, are cleaning up when you can get them down through the sweep without getting swept off the structure entirely.

The pattern holds at Sandy Point too, especially the last two hours of the incoming when bait gets funneled around the spit. I had a charter Sunday morning working the rip line off the point in 15 to 20 feet, and we picked at slot bass steadily on live bunker under a balloon, plus a couple of bluefish in the 6- to 8-pound class that showed up chopping bait on the surface — no surprise there, the blues are riding the same peanut bunker wave that's got stripers blitzing everywhere from Narragansett Bay up into Buzzards Bay this month. It's an unusual amount of visible bunker-driven activity for mid-August, honestly, more like an October pattern than what we usually see this time of year, and my read is it's early staging ahead of the fall push. Worth taking seriously if you're planning trips into September.

Here's the honest part: no bonito, no false albacore off Block Island yet. I've had my eyes on the water off North Light and out past Clay Head every trip this week, glassing for that telltale nervous water and diving terns, and it hasn't shown. The ingredients are all there — warm water pushing into the high 60s and low 70s across the region, bait stacked thick, and we're now two days past the new moon that typically kicks the current hard enough to bring albies and bonito ripping into the Block Island rips. Southeast Light and the rip off North Light are the first places they usually show when they do, so that's where I'd be running the spread of Deadly Dicks and small Albie Snax if you want to be the first one on them. My money says within the next week, once this tidal push settles into a rhythm, somebody's going to hook up off the island. I wouldn't build a whole trip around it yet, but I'd have the light tackle rigged and ready.

Fluke fishing has been fair, not great. We worked the drift off Sandy Point in 25 to 35 feet Thursday with white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, tipped with a fresh strip of squid, and put four keepers in the box against a lot of shorts. The bigger fish are still scattered — nothing like the doormat action other zones are seeing right now — so I'm treating fluke as a bonus fish this week rather than the target. Black sea bass, on the other hand, keep improving steadily on the reef structure south of the island in 60 to 80 feet. Green crab and squid combos on double bottom rigs are producing a solid mixed bag, and that trend should keep firming through the rest of August as water temps hold.

Looking ahead: I want to fish the SW Ledge slack again this weekend, ideally the Saturday evening tide when the moon's a little fuller and the current should run even harder through the rip. If the bunker stay stacked the way they have been, that's where the bigger bass will keep showing. And I'll be running out toward North Light and Southeast Light every trip looking for that first bonito flash — the water's right, the bait's right, it's just a matter of which morning it clicks. If I had one day to gamble on it, I'd pick a calm morning right around the next tide change and put the light spinning gear within casting range of that rip edge before the sun's even up.
